# From color labels to spin operations: three derivation routes

These optional workshops accompany the color-group, spin-only stabilizer and SOC-locking lessons in Spin and Extended Symmetries. Predict first and calculate manually; after inspecting the steps, change one condition to test your explanation.

## Color permutations and time reversal

A two-color label exchange can be extended formally to the linear matrix P=σx. For electron spin one-half, this site uses time reversal Θ=−iσyK, with K conjugating the complex amplitudes first. These are explicitly different action spaces; using two components does not make them the same physical object.

Compare Pψ, ψ*, Θψ and two successive applications. Then choose a complex scalar c and compare P(cψ)=cPψ with Θ(cψ)=c*Θψ. A real c can conceal the difference. After changing the operator phase, compute the antiunitary square AA*, rather than substituting the ordinary matrix square A².

Equal components, the same ray and orthogonality are different tests. The workshop provides both ⟨Pψ|Θψ⟩ and ⟨ψ|Θψ⟩. The exact counterexample H=σx preserves P but has two nondegenerate levels; it does not preserve Θ. Kramers pairing also requires the relevant antiunitary symmetry of the Hamiltonian. A same-momentum claim in a crystal additionally requires checking momentum.

The original three-color pattern experiment is a separate geometric comparison. Copying initializes its complete supported inputs and waits for a manual run; a two-component complex state is not treated as three colors.

## Spin-only stabilizers fixing every site

Arrange the ordered moments as M=[m₁ … mN] and determine their span using exact rank. A spin-only operation has identity spatial action: every moment must satisfy Wmᵢ=mᵢ at its original site. Preserving a pattern after permuting different sites does not meet this pointwise condition.

For a moment span of rank r, the full classical stabilizer is isomorphic to O(3−r). The workshop displays the span, its orthogonal complement, the projector and pointwise residuals for the selected W. Zero, collinear, coplanar and three-dimensional spans give O(3), O(2), the two-element plane-reflection group and the identity group, respectively. The unitary proper-rotation part is listed separately.

When det W=−1, take V=−W∈SO(3) and implement the classical action through D(V)Θ. The interface separately shows W², the spin-factor matrix and its antiunitary square: classical W²=I does not determine the sign of the spinor square. This spin factor excludes spatial-orbital and Bloch-phase actions and cannot alone diagnose band degeneracy.

This stabilizer calculation applies to the exactly specified input pattern. It does not classify near-coplanarity using measurement tolerances, search a full spin space group or verify a material Hamiltonian.

## Independent spin actions and SOC locking

First test the supplied independent combination [U∥R|t] on the same ordered structure. Then construct the ordinary unitary branch W=det(R)R and the branch with time reversal, W=−det(R)R, separately. Check positions, chemical labels and moments site by site.

The statements “candidate W equals the supplied U” and “candidate W preserves this pattern” are displayed separately. The first tests whether the original operation obeys the locking rule; the second checks pattern matching for a candidate operation. Failure of one ordinary unitary branch does not exclude a magnetic operation with time reversal. Neither test proves symmetry of a real SOC Hamiltonian.

Periodic models permit positions differing by integer lattice translations; finite point patterns are not periodically wrapped. Custom periodic inputs use a unit orthogonal lattice, whose spatial rotations must preserve the integer translation lattice. Unwrapped positions and target sites are retained together, so the finite displayed fragment is not mistaken for a complete space group.

## Inputs and results

Custom numbers accept bounded finite decimals and rational p/q values; expressions are not executed. Nonzero complex states and operator phases are normalized exactly. Custom orthogonal matrices must pass an exact check, which rounded rotation matrices may fail. At most 12 ordered sites or moments are accepted.

Exact strings are generated by rational and algebraic matrix calculations in Python; numerical mirrors support the three-dimensional display. Panel results can be exported separately. Copying to an original geometric experiment passes only its supported inputs and keeps the scope of the two calculations distinct.
